stem: What percentage of elderly patients with delirium will go on to develop dementia?
explanation: Among the elderly 10-15% of patients have delirium on admission, and a further 10-40% develop delirium during their hospital stay. Liposwski (1983) reported no detectable cause for delirium in between 5 and 20% of cases.

explanation: Dementia is a progressive syndrome affecting around 5% of those aged >65 years, rising to 20% in the over-80s. The most common cause of dementia is Alzheimer disease, accounting for around 60% of all cases.

explanation: Antipsychotics in the elderly have been associated with increased mortality (1-2% absolute risk), cerebrovascular events (rate ratio 1.73, range 1.6-1.87), metabolic side effects, and pneumonia. stem: The gene for amyloid precursor protein (APP) is on the long arm of chromosome
explanation: The gene for amyloid precursor protein (APP) is on the long arm of chromosome 21. The process of differential splicing yields four forms of the APP. stem: In elderly patients, what is the target serum lithium level for the treatment of bipolar disorder?
explanation: For adults with bipolar disorder, the standard lithium serum level should be 0.60-0.80mmol/L with the option to reduce it to 0.40- 0.60mmol/L in case of good response but poor tolerance, or to increase it to 0.80-1.00mmol/L in case of insufficient response and good tolerance. For the elderly, a more conservative approach may be adopted: usually 0.40-0.60mmol/L, with the option to go to maximally 0.70 or 0.80mmol/L at 65-79 years and to maximally 0.70mmol/L over 80 years.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 297.

stem: The 10-year probability of conversion from Mild Cognitive Impairment to dementia is
explanation: Mitchell and Shiri-Feshki (2009) conducted a meta-analysis of 41 high-quality studies and noted that the yearly conversion rate from MCI to dementia is around 5-10%; even after 10 years, only 40% (not the majority) of MCI patients will progress to dementia. Other meta-analyses of long-term (5-10 years) studies present still lower yearly conversion rates, varying between 3.3 – 4.2%, with cumulative conversion rates of ~31% over ten years (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19236314).

stem: A 79-year-old woman is admitted to the psychiatric ward while experiencing paranoid psychosis. She is started on chlorpromazine. How much higher is her risk for developing tardive dyskinesia compared to a 33-year-old woman treated for the same condition with the same dose?
explanation: Tardive dyskinesia is a common iatrogenic neurological and neurobehavioural syndrome associated with the use of antidopaminergic medication, especially antipsychotics. Age is a significant risk factor for the development of tardive dyskinesia. The older the patient, the greater the risk. There is up to a 6-fold greater incidence in those exposed to antipsychotics in mid- to late-life compared to younger adults.
reference: Owens DC. Tardive dyskinesia update: the syndrome. BJPsych Advances. 2019 Jan;25(1):57-69.

stem: What is the average life expectancy of patients diagnosed with Lewy body dementia?
explanation: Dementia with Lewy bodies is the third most common type of dementia (5-10%). It is characterised by progressive dementia with parkinsonism, as well as fluctuations in levels of attention and severity of cognitive impairment. Life expectancy/mean survival time after diagnosis is approximately 6 years, though it is variable (generally 5.5-7.7 years from disease onset, 1.9-6.3 years from diagnosis).
reference: Mueller C, Ballard C, Corbett A, Aarsland D. The prognosis of dementia with Lewy bodies. The Lancet Neurology. 2017 May 1;16(5):390-8.

Greater risk of developing tardive dyskinesia
Greater likelihood of formal thought disorder

stem: You are seeing a 76-year-old gentleman in the memory clinic. On routine blood tests, his calcium levels are noted to be high. Low levels of which of the following can artificially elevate calcium in the blood?
explanation:
The amount of total calcium varies with the level of serum albumin, a protein to which calcium is bound. So when albumin levels are low, free calcium levels will be high in the plasma as they are not bound to proteins. Therefore low levels of albumin can artificially elevate calcium levels in the blood. Low albumin levels (hypoalbuminaemia) may be caused by various conditions such as liver disease, nephrotic

syndrome, malabsorption, malnutrition (common in older people with dementia), burns, late pregnancy, artefact, genetic variations and malignancy.

stem: Which of the following is consistently found in normal ageing brains?
options: Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra and locus cereleus
Tau proteins in some nerve cells
Lipofuscin in the cytoplasm of nerve cells
Hirano bodies in new hippocampal pyramidal cells
explanation: Population-based autopsy studies of the brains of aged people without a neurological disease consistently report the presence of amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, Lewy bodies, inclusion of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), synaptic dystrophy, the loss of neurons, and the loss of brain volume in most of the brains. As well as classic protein deposits, other subcellular structures that accumulate in ageing brains (inside glial cells or neuronal cells) include stress granules, lipofuscin, Marinesco bodies, and Hirano bodies.
reference: Wyss-Coray T. Ageing, neurodegeneration and brain rejuvenation. Nature. 2016 Nov;539(7628):180-6.

options: It always responds well to neuroleptics.
It occurs in over 50% of patients at some stage in their illness.
It may present with sedation and hypoactivity.

Patients may become agitated or aggressive or alternatively, may present with hypoactive delirium. Antipsychotics may reduce the severity and duration of delirium or may further cloud the patient’s mental state.

stem: Of those listed, which personality disorder is most associated with suicide in older adults?
explanation: Obsessive-compulsive and avoidant personality disorders have been implicated in death by suicide in older adults, although this association may be confounded by depression. An inability to adapt to the changes occurring in late life may help to explain the association between suicide in old age and higher conscientiousness as well as obsessive-compulsive and avoidant personality disorders. Cluster B personality disorders and their defining constructs play a smaller role in late-life suicide compared to suicide in younger adults.
reference: Szücs A et al. Personality and suicidal behavior in old age: a systematic literature review. Frontiers in psychiatry. 2018 May 7;9:128.

explanation: A proportion of Pick's disease cases is familial though the majority are sporadic with no other family members being affected. stem: Which of the following is used for the differential diagnosis of cognitive dysfunction in older people?
explanation: The Cambridge Examination for Mental Disorders of the Elderly (CAMDEX-R) is a well-organised and generally comprehensive instrument for the differential diagnosis of dementia. CAMDEX was designed specifically for use in elderly people with the diagnosis of dementia and was later revised as CAMDEX-R. It includes a structured interview with the patient; a relative or other informant interview; a brief physical examination; and a neuropsychological test battery, the Cambridge Cognitive Assessment - Revised (CAMCOG-R).
reference: Hodges JR. Cognitive assessment for clinicians, 3rd Edition. 2018. pp. 158-161.

stem: Which scale is useful to obtain a differential diagnosis of dementia among the elderly?
explanation: The CAMDEX incorporates MMSE, Blessed dementia rating scale and Haschinski Ischemia score, in a comprehensive inquiry from the subject and informant. BDRS is a measure of activities of daily living. The Hachinksi Ischemia Score helps to differentiate between vascular and Alzheimer's dementia. A notable feature of CAMDEX is CAMCOG, which is the cognitive subscale. Trained non-doctors mainly use CAMDEX in research. (Seminars in old age psychiatry-14)

stem: Which of the following features is not required for a probable diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease according to the NINCDS/ADRDA Criteria? (National institute of neurological and communicative disorders and stroke/Alzheimer's disease and Related disorders association)
options: An absence of other disorders causing dementia
Abnormal cognitive function on formal testing
Cerebral atrophy on a CT head scan
correctAnswer: Cerebral atrophy on a CT head scan
explanation:
According to NINCDS-ADRDA criteria proposed in 1984, for a probable Alzheimer's disease, dementia should be established by clinical and neuropsychological examination. Cognitive impairments also have to be progressive and be present in 2 or more areas of cognition. The onset of the deficits has been between the ages of 40 and 90 years and finally there must be an absence of other diseases capable of

producing a dementia syndrome. For a definite diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, the patient should meet the criteria for probable Alzheimer's disease with histopathologic evidence of Alzheimer's disease (autopsy).

options: Cluster B disorders are the most common
Rates of personality disorders is highest among those with depression
Personality disorders can be diagnosed after the age of 65
Personality disorders contribute to treatment resistance in depression
Diogenes syndrome is considered as an end-stage of personality disorder

explanation: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a sporadic, progressive, neurodegenerative disease resulting clinically in a symmetrical Parkinson syndrome, prominent postural instability with falls, a vertical gaze palsy, and cognitive decline. stem: Which of the following clinical features is not consistent with an ICD-11 diagnosis of delirium?
explanation: Delirium is characterised by a disturbance of attention, orientation, and awareness that develops within a short period of time (e.g., within hours or days), typically presenting as significant confusion or global neurocognitive impairment, with transient symptoms that may fluctuate depending on the underlying causal condition or aetiology. In delirium, cognition is typically impaired in a global manner, such that multiple areas of neurocognitive functioning are impaired upon assessment. A disturbance of the sleep-wake cycle, including reduced arousal of acute onset or total sleep loss with reversal of the sleep-wake cycle, may also be present. Delirium often includes disturbance of emotion, including anxiety symptoms, depressed mood, irritability, fear, anger, euphoria, or apathy. stem: What is the most common psychological and behavioural symptom in patients with Huntington disease?
explanation: Apathy is ‘a quantifiable reduction in goal-directed behaviour’, manifesting clinically as a reduction in interest, spontaneity, motivation, and drive. It is the most frequent psychological and behavioural symptom in Huntington disease (HD), especially in the middle and later stages, causing a severe reduction in activities of daily living. With regard to cognitive and psychological symptoms, apathy and irritability are the two faces of the same coin. A patient can be apathetic in the morning and irritable in the afternoon, depending on the situation. As is the case for irritability, apathy can be caused by environmental and psychological issues. The estimated prevalence of neurotic disorders is between 1-10% with a female predominance. Non-specific anxiety symptoms, Hypochondriacal and depressive symptoms predominate. Multiple factors may contribute to new neurotic symptoms in the elderly. The most common ones are; physical illness, major life events, bereavement, social isolation,

impaired self-care and insecure personality factors.

stem: The neurotransmitters most often implicated in the pathophysiology of Alzheimer disease are
explanation: The neurotransmitters usually implicated in the pathophysiologic condition of Alzheimer disease (AD) are acetylcholine and norepinephrine, both of which are likely hypoactive in AD. Under normal circumstances, neurons in the basal nucleus of Meynert synthesise acetylcholine (ACh) and send axonal projections throughout the entire cerebral cortex and the limbic system to provide cholinergic innervation. Loss of neurons in the basal nucleus of Meynert characterises AD. As with the distribution of the macroscopic and microscopic changes in AD, ACh activity is particularly reduced in the cortical association areas and limbic system. AD is also associated with reduced concentrations of other established or putative neurotransmitters: somatostatin, substance P, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), vasopressin, and several other polypeptides. However, compared to the ACh loss, their concentrations are not decreased profoundly or consistently.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 240. Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 122.

stem: The most prevalent anxiety disorder among older adults is
explanation: The estimated prevalence of anxiety disorders in older adults is 4-14%. They are more common among women than men. Specific phobia is the most prevalent anxiety disorder among older adults; fear of falling is most common. Generalised anxiety disorder is one of the most common anxiety disorders in older adults; anxiety content reflects multiple issues that arise in later stages of life (e.g. health, welfare or loss of loved ones, life transitions, retirement, caregiving responsibilities), and economic and legal issues (e.g. reduced income, increased health care costs, end-of-life planning). explanation: There are no clear distinctions between the clinical presentation of depression in the elderly and that in younger patients. However, some symptoms are often more striking. Severe psychomotor retardation or agitation occurs in up to 30% of depressed elderly patients. Depressive delusions regarding poverty, physical illness, or nihilistic in nature are common. Classic symptoms may not be evident, and the patient may instead present with somatic, anxiety, or hypochondriacal complaints. stem: A 75-year-old man with Parkinson disease develops psychosis unrelated to levodopa use. Of those listed, which is the best antipsychotic for his treatment?
explanation: Clozapine, quetiapine, and pimavanserin have shown some efficacy in treating psychosis in Parkinson disease. Clozapine has the most robust evidence base. However, its use is limited by agranulocytosis risk and the associated need for blood count monitoring. In clinical practice, quetiapine is more readily used than clozapine, given its side effect profile compared to clozapine. Other neuroleptics have thus far demonstrated mixed results with increased risk of extrapyramidal worsening. The introduction of pimavanserin has provided another treatment option for Parkinson disease psychosis, decreasing concern for deterioration in motor function.
reference: Kyle K, Bronstein JM. Treatment of psychosis in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy Bodies: A review. Parkinsonism & Related Disorders. 2020 Jun 1;75:55-62.

stem: Which of the following best indicates the status of estrogen treatment in postmenopausal women with Alzheimer's disease?
options: RCTs find no improvement in the Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores
No RCTs have been conducted to examine the effects of estrogen in this clinical group
RCTs consistently show beneficial effects on activities of daily living
RCTs find an improvement in MMSE scores that is sustained for at least one year
RCTs find small short-term improvements in MMSE scores that do not translate to clinical benefit
correctAnswer: RCTs find small short-term improvements in MMSE scores that do not translate to clinical benefit
explanation:
A Cochrane systematic review identified five RCTs that included 210 postmenopausal women with Alzheimer disease. "The reviewers looked at various outcomes (such as MMSE, memory, concentration, and cognitive function) after treatment with different types of estrogen, at different doses, delivered by different routes and for different durations. Meta-analyses showed that there was a limited positive effect from low-dose conjugated equine estrogens (0.625 mg once a day) but not from a higher dose (1.25 mg of conjugated equine estrogens once a

day) on the MMSE after two months, but the effect disappeared after three, six, and 12 months of treatment. This effect was small and not clinically relevant". (http://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.0020031)

options: Loss of nerve cells in the hippocampus
Reduction in the weight of the brain
Reduction in cerebral blood flow in the frontal lobe
explanation:
Biological changes in the brain associated with ageing include: - Decrease in gross brain weight, about 17% by age 80 in both sexes

- Widened sulci, smaller convolutions, gyral atrophy - Ventricles enlarge - Increased transport across blood-brain barrier - Decreased cerebral blood flow and oxygenation

stem: Which of the following statements concerning pharmacokinetics in the elderly is true?
options: Renal blood flow decreases with age even in those with normal physical health
Total gastrointestinal drug absorption is reduced
25% of adult renal function is lost by 80 years
Serum creatinine measurement is the most accurate way of measuring renal function
correctAnswer: Renal blood flow decreases with age even in those with normal physical health
explanation:
How ageing affects drug therapy (pharmacokinetics): - Gut motility decreases with age, as does gastric acid secretion; drugs are absorbed more slowly but the same amount is absorbed

- Renal function declines with age; 35% of function is lost by 65 years and 50% by age 80 - Measurement of serum creatinine can be misleading because muscle mass is reduced, so less creatinine is produced

stem: A70 year old lady has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's dementia recently. What is the risk of same illness for her sister provided there is no other family history of Alzheimer's dementia?

correctAnswer: Risk will be three times higher
explanation:
The actual predicted risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in the first-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease is 15-19%, compared with 5% in controls. stem: Which class of antidepressants is generally used as first-line treatment for late-onset depression?
explanation: A Cochrane review examining the efficacy, and associated withdrawal rates, of different classes of antidepressants in older people found that SSRIs and tricyclics are of the same efficacy. However, TCAs are associated with higher withdrawal rates. NICE recommends starting with an SSRI (sertraline is commonly used first line in older people). There is no ideal antidepressant in older people, and all are associated with problems. TCAs are broadly considered less desirable due to the increased risk of cardiac conduction abnormalities and anticholinergic effects. SSRIs are generally better tolerated than TCAs; however, they increase the risk of bleeding. Older people are also particularly prone to develop hyponatraemia with SSRIs, as well as postural hypotension and falls.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 673-676.

explanation: The modified Hachinski Ischaemic Score (HIS) is used as a measure of the likelihood of vascular pathology based on the nature of dementia presentation and vascular risk factors. Clinically a score of greater than 4 on the HIS is indicative of a diagnosis of vascular dementia.

stem:
Diagnosis in the elderly For each of the following clinical conditions, match the most appropriate psychiatric syndrome from the given list:

A 77-year-old widowed gentleman became increasingly isolated over the last two years and has been neglecting himself of late. He lives in filthy, poor conditions which has triggered a referral to the local Choose... council and social services, but he is resistant to accept help. A 78-year-old lady with hearing impairment lives on her own believes that her neighbours are spying on her. She can also hear neighbours talking about her all the time through the walls. Choose...

A 83-year-old lady with bilateral cataracts sees animals and people in the house. She is relatively independent in terms of her daily activities and enjoys life in general. Choose...

A 87-year-old lady with a history of falls was brought to the A&E by the paramedics. She is agitated, paranoid, confused and also has visual hallucinations. She was previously reported to be a high functioning Choose... lady
correctAnswer: A 77-year-old widowed gentleman became increasingly isolated over the last two years and has been neglecting himself of late. He lives in filthy, poor conditions which has triggered a referral to the local council and social services, but he is resistant to accept help. → Diogenes syndrome, A 78-year-old lady with hearing impairment lives on her own believes that her neighbours are spying on her. She can also hear neighbours talking about her all the time through the walls. → Late onset paraphrenia, A 83-year-old lady with bilateral cataracts sees animals and people in the house. She is relatively independent in terms of her daily activities and enjoys life in general. → Charles Bonnet syndrome, A 87-year-old lady with a history of falls was brought to the A&E by the paramedics. She is agitated, paranoid, confused and also has visual hallucinations. She was previously reported to be a high functioning lady → Acute confusional state
explanation:
Case 1 is Diogenes syndrome (or 'senile squalor syndrome') refers to severe self-neglect seen in somewhat eccentric and reclusive elderly individuals. They become increasingly isolated and neglect themselves, living in filthy, poor conditions. It can be viewed as the response of someone with a particular personality type to the hardships of old age and loneliness (Howard & Bergman 1993). They are often oblivious to their condition and resistant to help, making management notoriously difficult as it is very hard to form a therapeutic alliance. Case 2 is late onset paraphrenia. Persecutory delusions are the most common symptoms of late paraphrenia; they are found in around 90% of patients. Auditory hallucinations occur in approximately 75% of cases. Visual hallucinations are observed in up to 60% of patients. Few patients may present with delusions only (10-20%). Partition delusions (attack through the wall, neighbours spying via any 'partition') are common. According to ICD-10, patients must either be diagnosed as having delusional disorder or schizophrenia - no separate diagnosis exists for paraphrenia.

Case 3 is a typical presentation of Charles Bonnet syndrome. Case 4 is delirium. The salient features include rapid onset of clinical features with fluctuations in severity over minutes and hours (even back to apparent normality), clouding of consciousness with reduced attention span and distractibility, global impairment of cognition with disorientation, and impairment of recent memory and abstract thinking.

Rating scales in old age psychiatry Identify the best fitting rating scales that could be used in each of the following situations.

This scale is more useful for the elderly as it focuses on cognitive and subjective symptoms more than physical symptoms Choose...

This scale is helpful to detect depression in people with dementia Choose...

This scale is especially useful for older hearing-impaired subjects Choose...

This scale is helpful for screening people with dementia Choose...

This scale has a number of somatic items, which renders it less appropriate for older subjects. Choose...
correctAnswer: This scale is more useful for the elderly as it focuses on cognitive and subjective symptoms more than physical symptoms → Geriatric depression scale, This scale is helpful to detect depression in people with dementia → Cornell scale for depression, This scale is especially useful for older hearing-impaired subjects → BASDEC, This scale is helpful for screening people with dementia → MMSE, This scale has a number of somatic items, which renders it less appropriate for older subjects. → Hamilton Rating Scale
explanation:
1) Geriatric Depression Scale: Originally a 30-item test, it now has 15-items that enable most subjects to be scored for depression in four or five minutes. It avoids somatic questions and so remains useful for older patients. An overall score of five or more suggests the possibility of a depressive episode. 2) Cornell scale for depression is the best validated scale for detecting depression in dementing patients. It is an interviewer-administered scale that uses information both from the patient and an outside informant. 3) BASDEC (Brief assessment schedule depression cards): It was initially designed for use in liaison psychiatry and is particularly useful with deaf subjects. It consists of a series of statements in large print on cards, which are shown to the patient, one at a time and answers 'true' or 'false'.

4) The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) is the standard screening instrument for dementia. It takes 5-10 minutes to administer and has a median positive Likelihood Ratio of 6.3 and a median Negative Likelihood Ratio of 0.19. It is a brief tool for grading cognitive impairment in elderly and screening for dementia. It is not very sensitive to change but used in the clinical trials for dementia. 5) It is a 30-point scale. It does not pick up frontal executive defects. Hamilton rating scale: It has a number of somatic items, which render it less appropriate for older subjects. It is more useful for working-age adults in quantifying depression.

Alzheimer's disease and neuroimaging Identify the most likely findings seen in Alzheimer's disease

CT scan Choose...

SPECT Scan Choose...

PET Scan Choose...

Magnetic resonance spectroscopy Choose...
correctAnswer: CT scan → Cortical atrophy in parietal and temporal lobes, SPECT Scan → Reduced cerebral blood flow in the temporal and posterior parietal lobes, PET Scan → Reduction in oxygen and glucose metabolism in temporal and posterior parietal lobes, Magnetic resonance spectroscopy → Reduced levels of N-Acetyl aspartate
explanation:
CT scan shows cortical atrophy especially over parietal and temporal lobes, and dilatation of the third ventricle, which correlates with cognitive impairment (most common picture). In the advanced stage of the disease, the frontal lobe is affected.

SPECT measures cerebral blood flow and in Alzheimer's disease, there is a characteristic reduction in blood flow in temporal and parietal regions. SPECT could distinguish specific features of dementia of Alzheimer type at early stages and frontal lobe dementia. PET scan measures oxygen and glucose metabolism directly. In Alzheimer's disease, there is 20-30% reduction in oxygen and glucose metabolism in temporal and posterior parietal lobes. In Magnetic resonance spectroscopy, there is an abnormal synthesis of membrane phospholipids early in the disease and reduced levels of N-Acetyl aspartate.

explanation: 1) For patients with a history of poor compliance with oral medications, depot antipsychotics could be considered. 2) Offer clozapine to patients with schizophrenia whose illness has not responded adequately to treatment despite the sequential use of at least two different antipsychotic drugs, one of which should be a second-generation antipsychotic drug. 3)In Parkinson's disease psychosis, try an atypical antipsychotic. Subtypes of dementia (1) For each of the following descriptions choose the most appropriate diagnosis from the list shown:

A 70-year-old gentleman has a history of hypertension, recurrent TIAs, has a three-year history of step-wise deterioration in cognitive functions. On examination, he has spastic weakness of left lower limbs and an extensor plantar response. He retains good insight and there is no impairment Choose... of personality. A 65-year-old gentleman has a ten months history of cognitive impairment, fluctuating levels of consciousness and prominent visual hallucination. He developed severe tremor and rigidity on Choose... small dose of Haloperidol 46-year-old gentleman presents with a history of worsening memory. On examination, there is increased tone with rigidity and abnormal jerky movements were present. There is also a strong Choose... family history of dementia.

A 67-year-old gentleman presenting with memory problems and urinary incontinence. On neurological examination, he has a broad-based, short stepped gait. A CT brain scan shows ventricular enlargement. Choose...
correctAnswer: A 70-year-old gentleman has a history of hypertension, recurrent TIAs, has a three-year history of step-wise deterioration in cognitive functions. On examination, he has spastic weakness of left lower limbs and an extensor plantar response. He retains good insight and there is no impairment of personality. → Multi-infarct dementia, A 65-year-old gentleman has a ten months history of cognitive impairment, fluctuating levels of consciousness and prominent visual hallucination. He developed severe tremor and rigidity on small dose of Haloperidol → Lewy body Dementia, 46-year-old gentleman presents with a history of worsening memory. On examination, there is increased tone with rigidity and abnormal jerky movements were present. There is also a strong family history of dementia. → Dementia in Huntington's disease, A 67-year-old gentleman presenting with memory problems and urinary incontinence. On neurological examination, he has a broad-based, short stepped gait. A CT brain scan shows ventricular enlargement. → Normal pressure hydrocephalus
explanation:
1) Multi-infarct dementia is a type of vascular dementia characterised by a history of recurrent strokes/TIAs, step-wise deterioration in cognitive functions. Often patients present with positive neurological signs. 2) Lewy body dementia presents as progressive cognitive decline interfering with normal social or occupational function along with fluctuating cognition with profound variations in attention and alertness, recurrent visual hallucinations that are typically well-formed and detailed, and spontaneous motor features of parkinsonism. Other symptoms supporting the diagnosis include repeated falls, syncope, and transient loss of consciousness, neuroleptic sensitivity, systematised delusions and hallucinations in other modalities.

3) Huntington's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with chorea and dystonia, incoordination, cognitive decline, and behavioural difficulties. The onset of symptoms is often in middle-age after affected individuals have had children. 4) Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus is a syndrome where there is dilatation of cerebral ventricles (especially 3rd ventricle) and normal CSF pressure at lumbar puncture. It typically presents with the triad of dementia, gait ataxia, and urinary incontinence.

Differential diagnosis of dementia For each of the following descriptions choose the most appropriate diagnosis from the list above

A 68-year-old gentleman is presenting with memory problems, history of recurrent falls, depressed mood and tremors involving both his upper limbs for the last three years. On examination, there is Choose... marked psychomotor retardation and has cogwheel rigidity A 69-year-old woman is presenting with flattened mood and is becoming increasingly withdrawn. Her memory is reported to be poor. While attempting to do MMSE, she was uncooperative and Choose... frequently responds saying 'I don't know '. A 64 year-old-gentleman is presenting with memory loss and disinhibited behaviour. CT brain shows knife blade atrophy of frontal and temporal lobes. Choose...

An 81-year-old lady admitted to the medical ward with a history of headache, drowsy and altered levels of consciousness. She has a history of previous hospitalisation with recurrent episodes of falls. The family has noticed physical slowness and sluggishness and also gave an account of Choose... deterioration in her cognitive functioning over the last few months
correctAnswer: A 68-year-old gentleman is presenting with memory problems, history of recurrent falls, depressed mood and tremors involving both his upper limbs for the last three years. On examination, there is marked psychomotor retardation and has cogwheel rigidity → Dementia in Parkinson's disease., A 69-year-old woman is presenting with flattened mood and is becoming increasingly withdrawn. Her memory is reported to be poor. While attempting to do MMSE, she was uncooperative and frequently responds saying 'I don't know '. → Depressive pseudodementia, A 64 year-old-gentleman is presenting with memory loss and disinhibited behaviour. CT brain shows knife blade atrophy of frontal and temporal lobes. → Dementia in Pick's disease, An 81-year-old lady admitted to the medical ward with a history of headache, drowsy and altered levels of consciousness. She has a history of previous hospitalisation with recurrent episodes of falls. The family has noticed physical slowness and sluggishness and also gave an account of deterioration in her cognitive functioning over the last few months → Chronic subdural haematoma
explanation:
1) This is a case of Parkinson's disease dementia. If both motor symptoms and cognitive symptoms develop within 12 months, then it is conventional to give a diagnosis of Lewy body dementia. If the parkinsonian symptoms have existed for more than 12 months before dementia develops then a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease dementia is given. 2) Depression in elderly patients may present as dementia clinically, which is known as depressive pseudo-dementia. These patients themselves complain of memory problems, difficulty in sustaining attention & concentration and reduced intellectual capacity.

3) Dementia in Pick's disease has an insidious onset and gradual progression, early loss of personal and social awareness, early emotional blunting and an early loss of insight. CT brain scan shows bilateral asymmetrical atrophy of frontal and temporal lobes, also called as knife- blade atrophy. 4) Chronic subdural haematoma is relatively more common in old age. In older people, as the brain shrinks the veins, which lie in between it and skull, can get torn easily even after minor trauma. SDH should be borne in mind where there is a changing pattern in cognitive function, especially if risk factors for SDH exist. The important risk factors are post trauma; elderly after a fall; elderly after a head injury, infancy, cerebral atrophy, alcoholism, epilepsy, clotting disorders, pre-disposing drugs such as aspirin, warfarin, etc.

This is subcortical dementia with a clinical course characterised by gradual intellectual decline, generalised slowing, and motor problems. MRI scan shows multiple microvascular infarcts and white Choose... matter leukoaraiosis The disease in humans affects mainly young men in their 20s and is characterised by early anxiety and depressive symptoms, followed by personality changes, and finally progressive dementia. Ataxia Choose... and myoclonus are prominent.

This condition typically presents with the triad of dementia, gait ataxia, and urinary incontinence. Choose...

The disease usually presents as a progressive frontal dementia. Classic symptoms would include grandiosity, euphoria, and mania with mood-congruent delusions. Disinhibition, personality change, Choose... and memory impairment are also common.
correctAnswer: This is subcortical dementia with a clinical course characterised by gradual intellectual decline, generalised slowing, and motor problems. MRI scan shows multiple microvascular infarcts and white matter leukoaraiosis → Binswanger's disease, The disease in humans affects mainly young men in their 20s and is characterised by early anxiety and depressive symptoms, followed by personality changes, and finally progressive dementia. Ataxia and myoclonus are prominent. → New variant CJD, This condition typically presents with the triad of dementia, gait ataxia, and urinary incontinence. → Normal pressure hydrocephalus, The disease usually presents as a progressive frontal dementia. Classic symptoms would include grandiosity, euphoria, and mania with mood-congruent delusions. Disinhibition, personality change, and memory impairment are also common. → General paresis of insane
explanation:
Case 1 is Binswanger's disease (progressive small vessel disease). It is subcortical dementia with a clinical course characterised by slow intellectual decline and generalised slowing. MRI scan shows small distinct infarcts (lacunae) or more widespread white matter changes (leukoariasis). Case 2 is new variant CJD. The rise of vCJD followed an epidemic of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle. The disease in humans affects mainly young men in their 20s and is characterised by early anxiety and depressive symptoms, followed by personality changes, and finally progressive dementia. Ataxia and myoclonus are prominent and the typical course is 1-2 yrs until death. Case 3 is Normal pressure hydrocephalus. NPH is a syndrome where there is dilatation of cerebral ventricles, especially the third ventricle) and normal CSF pressure at lumbar puncture. It typically presents with the triad of dementia, gait ataxia, and urinary incontinence.

Case 4 is General Paresis of insane (GPI). It is an impairment of mental function caused by damage to the brain from untreated syphilis. This damage can produce hallucinations and delusions (grandiosity). Brief, sharp "lightning" pains occur with tabes dorsalis. Eye changes including abnormal pupil response, mood changes (euphoria and mania), overactive reflexes, personality changes and speech changes are also noted. General paresis usually begins about 15 - 20 years after the syphilis infection. Cerebral atrophy and gliosis, dominantly in the frontal lobes are well-known neuropathological findings of GPI.

Psychiatric side effects of non-psychiatric medications For each of the side effect profile given below identify the possible offending drug

A 74-year-old gentleman being treated for resting tremors develops acute confusional state with paranoia and visual hallucinations Choose...

A 67-year-old lady was taking treatment for swollen legs complaints of visual halos, which are green in colour and appears to be confused. Choose...

A 56-year-old woman on treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica becomes hypomanic and confused. Choose...

A 79-year-old man treated for ventricular tachycardia became confused, agitated and presented with paranoid delusions Choose...
correctAnswer:
A 74-year-old gentleman being treated for resting tremors develops acute confusional state with paranoia and visual hallucinations → Levodopa, A 67-year-old lady was taking treatment for swollen legs complaints of visual halos, which are green in colour

and appears to be confused. → Digoxin, A 56-year-old woman on treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica becomes hypomanic and confused. → Prednisolone, A 79-year-old man treated for ventricular tachycardia became confused, agitated and presented with paranoid delusions → Amiodarone
explanation: The patient in scenario 1 is likely to be taking treatment for Parkinson's disease using levodopa. Levodopa is associated with high rates of visual hallucinations. Other psychiatric side effects of Levodopa consist of psychosis, hallucinations, confusion, euphoria, depression, insomnia and abnormal dreams. The patient in scenario 2 is likely to be suffering from cardiac failure and is taking digoxin. One of the side effects of cardiac glycosides such as digoxin is a change in vision characterised by seeing a halo or light around objects. The patient in scenario 3 is likely to be taking steroids for her autoimmune condition. Corticosteroids are commonly implicated in iatrogenic depression, mania or hypomania and confusion. Amiodarone is used for the treatment of refractory ventricular tachycardia (scenario 4). The psychiatric side effects include altered mental status, hallucinations, and delirium that have been reported mainly among older subjects.

explanation:
1) This patient has a cerebral tumour which causes symptoms common to all space occupying lesions and consequent upon raised intracranial pressure (headache, early morning nausea, vomiting, impaired cognition, apathy, emotional blunting, altered consciousness and

brain herniation syndromes). Some of these compression symptoms could be treated with corticosteroids such as dexamethasone, which can reduce cerebral oedema and relieve pressure symptoms. However, surgical evacuation would be the best treatment of choice for patients with cerebral tumour. 2) This patient has developed hepatic failure due to chronic alcoholism, a fluctuating chronic organic state in which physical and psychiatric symptoms wax and wane in unison. The physical symptoms include flapping tremor of hands (asterixis), motor retardation, ataxia, hyperreflexia, clonus & coma. Neomycin and lactulose are used for the treatments of hepatic encephalopathy. 3) This is a case of normal pressure hydrocephalus, featured by dementia, urinary incontinence and gait ataxia. Treatment most commonly requires the insertion of a shunt between the lateral ventricles and the inferior vena cavae and this may alleviate even severe degrees of dementia (Bekkelund at al 1999). 4) The diagnosis is general paresis of insane (GPI) due to neurosyphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum. Antibiotic therapy prevents disease progression. Neurosyphilis is treated with intramuscular procaine penicillin for 10-21 days.

A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic now presents with apathy, fatigue, irritability, depression and cognitive impairment. Choose...

A 76-year-old woman with atrophic gastritis now presents with fatigue, tingling and numbness of hands & feet, depression and memory problems. Choose...

A 57-year-old woman presents with mouth ulcers, diarrhoea, lassitude, impaired cognition, depression and dementia Choose...

A 45-year-old woman with lethargy, excessive tiredness, constipation, low mood and memory problems. Choose...
correctAnswer: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic now presents with apathy, fatigue, irritability, depression and cognitive impairment. → Thiamine, A 76-year-old woman with atrophic gastritis now presents with fatigue, tingling and numbness of hands & feet, depression and memory problems. → Vitamin B12, A 57-year-old woman presents with mouth ulcers, diarrhoea, lassitude, impaired cognition, depression and dementia → Folate supplements, A 45-year-old woman with lethargy, excessive tiredness, constipation, low mood and memory problems. → Thyroxine
explanation:
1) The diagnosis is chronic thiamine deficiency due to alcoholism. Acute thiamine depletion causes Wernicke's encephalopathy and later, Korsakoff's psychosis. Chronic thiamine deficiency causes apathy, fatigue, irritability, depression and cognitive impairment prior to the development of classical beriberi. 2) The diagnosis is vitamin B 12 deficiency (Pernicious anemia). The typical symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency anemia include diarrhoea or constipation, fatigue, loss of appetite, pale skin, problems concentrating, swollen, red tongue or bleeding gums. Monthly vitamin B12 injections are prescribed to correct the vitamin B12 deficiency. 3) The diagnosis is folate deficiency. It may cause diarrhoea, grey hair, mouth ulcers and peptic ulcers. It may be associated with lassitude, impaired cognition, depression and dementia (prolonged deficiency). The treatment would be replacement with folic acid supplements and fortified foods, to ensure the proper daily intake.

4) This is hypothyroidism, caused by low thyroxine levels due to thyroid disease, thyroidectomy or drugs. There is a strong family history. → Huntington's disease, A 25-year-old man with jaundice, wing-beating tremor of shoulders, rigidity, and memory problems → Wilson's disease
explanation: 1) The diagnosis is Progressive Supranuclear Palsy. The onset is in the sixth decade (range 45 to 75 years]. It presents with difficulty in balance, abrupt falls, slurred speech, dysphagia, and vague changes in personality, sometimes with an apprehensiveness and fretfulness suggestive of an agitated depression. The most common early complaint is unsteadiness of gait and unexplained falling (retropulsion). 2) Huntington's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with chorea and dystonia, incoordination, cognitive decline, and behavioural difficulties. The onset of symptoms is often in middle-age after affected individuals have had children. 3) The diagnosis is Wilson's disease. The onset is usually in adolescence or early childhood. Clinical features include liver cirrhosis, tremor, dystonia, flapping tremor of wrists, wing-beating tremor of shoulders, and Kayser-Fleischer rings (greenish brown corneal deposits). Mood disturbances are common and subcortical dementia is seen in 25% of cases.

explanation: 1) Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is caused by the reactivation of a common virus in the central nervous system of immune-compromised individuals. PML is usually seen in people with AIDS, and those undergoing chronic corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy and individuals with cancer, such as Hodgkin's disease, lymphoma, and sarcoidosis. The most prominent symptoms are clumsiness; progressive weakness; cognitive impairment, problems with coordination and visual impairment, speech disturbances and sometimes personality changes. The progression of deficits leads to life-threatening disability and death over weeks to months. (Ref: www.ninds.nih.gov). 2) Patients with Lewy body dementia have a history of Parkinsonism and are very sensitive to antipsychotic medications. 3) In sporadic CJD, most cases occur after the fifth decade, although onset can occur at any age. The clinical picture is one of rapidly deteriorating dementia, myoclonus, cerebellar and extrapyramidal signs leading to death within a year. Patients may present with non- specific symptoms such as lethargy, depression and fatigue. Within weeks, more fulminant symptoms develop, including progressive cortical-pattern dementia, myoclonus and pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs. Myoclonus becomes prominent as the disease progresses. Patients may develop cortical blindness.

1) Diagnosis is Alzheimer's disease. CT/MRI shows medial temporal lobe atrophy and parietal atrophy. 2) The diagnosis is Lewy body dementia. 3) Diagnosis is a fronto-temporal type of dementia. CT/MRI shows atrophy of both cerebrum and cerebellum. 5) The diagnosis is vascular dementia. MRI scan shows global atrophy, focal white matter lesions, lacunes and strategic infarcts (infarcts in regions that are involved in cognitive function).

A 53-year-old man is unable to direct eye movements voluntarily but has normal reflex eye movements. → Progressive supranuclear palsy, A 37-year-old woman with fulminant liver failure and abnormal movements → Wilson's disease, A 79-year-

old gentleman with psychomotor slowness, memory loss and gradual intellectual decline → Binswanger's disease
explanation:
1) Progressive supranuclear palsy- The most common early complaint is unsteadiness of gait and unexplained falling (retropulsion). It may take a year or longer for the characteristic syndrome-comprising supranuclear ophthalmoplegia, pseudo bulbar palsy, and axial dystonia to develop fully. Difficulty in the voluntary vertical movement of the eyes (vertical gaze palsy). Bell's phenomenon (reflexive upturning of eyes

on forced closure of the eyelids) and the ability to converge are also lost eventually, and the pupils then become small. 2) Wilson's disease- It is a rare autosomal recessive, progressive, but eminently treatable disorder of copper metabolism, causing a personality change, cognitive decline, and extrapyramidal disorder and cirrhosis of the liver. The extrapyramidal features include tremor, dysarthria, drooling, rigidity and bradykinesia. Kayser-Fleischer rings (copper deposits on Descemet's membrane of the cornea) are present in 95% of patients with neurological symptoms. 3) Progressive small vessel disease (Binswanger's disease)- This is subcortical dementia with a clinical course characterised by slow intellectual decline and generalised slowing. The clinical picture can be dominated by dementia, and there may be concomitant physical problems such as gait disorders or dysarthria. MRI scan shows small distinct infarcts (Lacunae) or more generalised white matter changes (Leukoariasis). Depression and Pseudobulbar palsy are not uncommon.

Choice of Antidementia Drugs (2) Identify the most appropriate drug/drugs for each of the following situations: 1. A 76-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease developed diarrhea on taking rivastigmine. He feels that the medication is helpful and resists changing his medication.

2. A 77-year-old man has been diagnosed with mixed dementia. He is disappointed to know that antidementia drugs are not indicated for the management of mixed dementia. He is keen on herbal remedies

3. A 79-year-old man has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. He has a significant history of cardiovascular disease and is on numerous medications.

4. A 73-year-old man with Alzheimer's dementia has read about the side effects of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, He would like to try the drug with minimal side effects.

5. The family doctor (General Practitioner) of a 79-year-old man with vascular dementia seeks your advice on treating the vascular risk factors. (Choose TWO)
explanation:
1) Rivastigmine transdermal patch is unlikely to cause any gastrointestinal side effects. Therefore, it could be used in these situations where the patient is not keen to change his medications, as he/she is benefitting out of it. 2) Gingko Biloba has been widely used as a cognitive enhancer. It is effective in mild to moderate Alzheimer's dementia with an advantage over placebo of around 1.4 points on ADAS-Cog. 3) Rivastigmine may be the safest choice in patients with cardiovascular disease given its lack of interaction potential with other drugs. 4) Donepezil is well tolerated and widely used. Rivastigmine and Galantamine appear more likely to cause gastrointestinal (GI) and neuropsychiatric adverse effects than does Donepezil. 5) Treatment of vascular risk factors aggressively is part of the management options of vascular dementia. It includes low dose aspirin, statins to reduce cholesterol, optimization of diabetic control and optimization of blood pressure.

Correct Answer is : 1. Rivastigmine transdermal patch 2. Gingko Biloba 3. Rivastigmine 4. Donepezil 5. Low dose aspirin, Statins

Clinical features of dementias Choose the most salient clinical features for each item below:

1. Lewy body dementia (3 Answers)

2. Frontotemporal dementia (3 answers)

3. Vascular dementia (2 answers)

4. A neurological feature associated with rapidly evolving fatal dementia
explanation:
1) The core features of dementia with Lewy bodies include Spontaneous motor features of Parkinsonism, progressive cognitive decline, recurrent visual hallucinations, which are typically well-formed and detailed. The supportive features include fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, neuroleptic sensitivity and history of falls. 2) Frontotemporal dementia: Features include Insidious onset and gradual progression, Early loss of personal and social awareness, Early emotional blunting, Early loss of insight. Behavioural features include early signs of disinhibition, a decline in personal hygiene & grooming, mental rigidity, inflexibility, hyperorality, stereotyped and perseverative behaviour. Speech disorder includes reduction and stereotypy of

speech, echolalia, and perseveration. Affective symptoms include Anxiety, depression, and frequent mood changes, emotional indifference. Physical signs include Incontinence, primitive reflexes, akinesia, rigidity and tremor. 3) Vascular dementia: Onset may usually follow a cerebrovascular event and is more acute in onset. The course is usually stepwise, with periods of intervening stability. Focal neurological signs & symptoms or neurological evidence of cerebrovascular disease (CVD) judged etiologically related to the disturbance. 4) Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: The clinical picture is one of rapidly deteriorating dementia, myoclonus, cerebellar and extrapyramidal signs leading to death within a year. Patients may present with non-specific symptoms such as lethargy, depression and fatigue. Within weeks, more fulminant symptoms develop, including progressive cortical-pattern dementia, myoclonus and pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs. Myoclonus becomes prominent as the disease progresses. Patients may develop cortical blindness.

Correct Answer is : 1. Motor features of Parkinson's disease, Visual hallucinations, Fluctuating levels of consciousness 2. Insidious onset and gradual progression, Personality change and behavioural disorder, Striking loss of insight 3. Stepwise deterioration , History of transient ischemic attacks 4. Myoclonus

Neuropsychometric assessments in dementia identify 2 tests commonly used by neuropsychologists in the detailed evaluation of cognitive functions

1. Tests of executive function

2. Tests for practically useful episodic memory linked to daily functioning

3. Measurement of IQ using non-verbal methods

4. Useful measure of severity of dementia

5. Useful to differentiate vascular from other causes of dementia
explanation:
1) Wisconsin card sorting test, Stroop test, Tower of London test, and controlled word association test are some of the tests of executive functioning. 2) Rivermead Behavioural Memory Test is used to identify everyday memory problems and monitor change over time, and assess a wider range of ability.

3) Ravens progressive matrices measures non-verbal intelligence. 4) Scales used to assess the severity of cognitive impairment include the commonly used MMSE and CAMDEX. CAMDEX stands for Cambridge examination for mental disorders of the elderly. CAMDEX incorporates the MMSE, Blessed dementia rating scale (BDRS) and the Hachinksi Ischaemia score in a comprehensive inquiry from the subject and informant. BDRS is a measure of activities of daily living. 5) The Hachinski ischaemia score is helpful to differentiate between Alzheimer's and vascular dementia. A notable feature of CAMDEX is CAMCOG, which is the cognitive subscale.

Correct Answer is : 1. Wisconsin card sorting test, Stroop test 2. Rivermead Behavioural Memory test 3. Ravens progressive matrices 4. Mini- mental state examination, CAMDEX 5. Hachinski index

Aetiology of dementias Identify 2 types of dementias for each etiological category given below

1. Degenerative cause

2. Intracranial

3. Infectious cause

4. Endocrine

5. Toxins
explanation:
1) Degenerative dementias include Alzheimer's disease, Picks disease, Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia, Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, motor neuron disease, progressive supranuclear palsy and multiple sclerosis.

2) Intracranial lesions causing dementia syndrome includes subdural haematoma, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, tumour and head injury. 3) Infectious cause include Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, HIV-associated dementia, neurosyphilis, tuberculosis. 4) Endocrine causes include hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, Cushing's syndrome and Addison's disease. 5) Toxins such as prolonged alcohol misuse, heavy metal poisoning and metabolic causes such as uraemia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, calcium imbalance and magnesium imbalance can also result in a dementia syndrome.

Correct Answer is : 1. Alzheimer's disease, Pick's disease 2. Subdural haematoma, Normal pressure hydrocephalus 3. HIV-associated dementia, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease 4. hypothyroidism, Hyperparathyroidism 5. Prolonged alcohol misuse, Heavy metal poisoning

Cortical and subcortical dementias Identify the common clinical features seen in each of the following types of dementias

1. Cortical dementias (Choose TWO)

2. Subcortical dementias (Choose THREE)
explanation:
Features of cortical dementias include early aphasia, acalculia and significant memory loss in early stages. Examples of cortical dementia include Alzheimer's disease, Pick's disease, etc. Subcortical dementias usually have no aphasia. The calculation is preserved until late, but the speed of cognitive processing is slowed early.

Other features include the appearance of depressed mood, dysarthric speech, slowed motor speed & control, bowed or extended posture, apathetic personality, adventitious movements like tics, chorea, tremors and dystonia. Examples of subcortical dementias include Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, etc.

Correct Answer is : 1. Early aphasia, Early loss of calculation ability 2. Adventitious movements, Depressed mood, Early slowing of cognitive processing

Vascular dementias Identify 3 appropriate clinical features for each of the different types of vascular dementias given below:

1. Multi-infarct dementia

2. Binswanger disease

3. CADASIL
explanation:
1) Multi-infarct dementia has an abrupt onset with a history of multiple strokes. It is associated with a stepwise deterioration in cognitive function. Between strokes, there are periods of relative stability. There are often risk factors for cardiovascular disease. 2) Progressive small vessel disease (Binswanger's disease) is subcortical dementia with a clinical course characterised by slow intellectual decline and generalised slowing. 3) CADASIL stands for Cerebral Autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy. It is a form of vascular dementia, and the disease is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait with high penetrance. Molecular genetic linkage studies have assigned the disease gene to the long arm of chromsome 19. Patients with this condition usually present with a recurrent stroke around later forties and there is often a history of migraine. Many patients later develop subcortical dementia and pseudo bulbar palsy. MRI shows widespread white matter changes. (Ref: http://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/pdf/semOAP_ch5.pdf (accessed July 01, 2015).

Correct Answer is : 1. Abrupt in onset, Stepwise deterioration in cognition, Follows a number of minor ischemic episodes 2. Gradual intellectual decline , Subcortical dementia, Generalised slowing 3. Onset in their 40s, Subcortical dementia, History of migraines

Dementia care You are seeing 3 different patients in your memory clinic. A dementia nurse at your clinic would like to seek advice and discuss options for some of his patients. Choose the most appropriate treatment options for the following presentation.

1. A 77-year-old man with MMSE score of 20/30 is unable to tolerate Donepezil. (Choose 2 answers)

2. A 82 year old woman with MMSE score of 9/30 presents with severe behavioural problems in a residential home (Choose 2 answers)

3. A 83 year old man has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's dementia. He is on a number of different medications for physical health problems. He would like to take a memory tablet which won't interact with his other medications

4. A 77-year-old man with vascular dementia. He is keen to try herbal preparations for his memory problems
explanation:
1) If a patient does not tolerate donepezil, they can try other drugs of the same class like galantamine and rivastigmine. 2) Memantine is recommended for moderate to severe dementia with behavioural problems. Risperidone is licensed for the treatment of behavioural problems of dementia in UK. 3) Drug-drug interaction is unlikely with rivastigmine. It is metabolised at the site of action and dose not affect hepatic cytochromes.

4) Gingko Biloba is a Chinese herbal preparation used for the treatment of mild dementia. However, the evidence is weak for its efficacy.

Correct Answer is : 1. Rivastigmine, Galantamine 2. Risperidone, Memantine 3. Rivastigmine 4. Gingko Biloba
